chunks: A retainer of Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) told me, saying:

One of his followers fell ill, so we went out to visit him — we were a group from among the followers of Ja'far. Then Ja'far (peace be upon him) met us on the road and said to us: 'Where are you headed?' We said: 'We are going to visit so-and-so.' He said to us: 'Stop.' So we stopped.

He said: 'Does one of you have an apple, or a quince, or a citron, or a spoonful of perfume, or a piece of incense?' We said: 'We have none of these with us.' He said: 'Do you not know that a sick person is comforted by every single thing that is brought in to him?'

key_terms.أُتْرُجَّة: Citron — a fragrant citrus fruit frequently mentioned in hadith for its pleasant aroma and medicinal properties
key_terms.عِيَادَة: Visiting the sick (implied by نعوده) — a recommended act in Islamic practice
key_terms.مَوَالِي: Followers/retainers (mawali) — those bound by ties of loyalty or patronage to the Imam
key_terms.يَسْتَرِيحُ: Finds comfort/relief — the patient's emotional and psychological ease from the visitor's gift

ai.seo_question: What should you bring when visiting a sick person according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) encounters a group of his followers on their way to visit a sick person. He stops them and asks if they are bringing any gift — a fruit, perfume, or incense — and upon learning they have nothing, gently admonishes them with the teaching that a patient finds comfort in anything brought to them. This hadith establishes the etiquette of sick visitation (ziyarat al-marid) in Shia Islam, emphasizing that bringing even a small gift is a Sunnah that provides both physical and emotional relief to the ill.
